a, b = A(), A()

assert b.items == [1] and A.items == [1]

The class body executes once at class creation, so a list made there is a single shared object.
replies.assert:
count = 0
class A:
    global count
    count += 1
    items = []
A(); A()
assert count == 1
assert A().items is A().items

A class attribute is looked up through the class, so all instances see the same value. An instance that assigns its own attribute of the same name shadows it, but the attribute set on the class is still shared.
replies.assert:
class A:
    x = 1
a, b = A(), A()
A.x = 5
assert a.x == 5 and b.x == 5

a, b = A(), A()
a.x = 1
assert a.x == 1 and not hasattr(b, 'x')

Calling a class creates an instance and runs __init__ on it with the arguments.
Inside __init__, self is the new instance, and assigning self.name stores an attribute on it.
replies.assert:
class Fox:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.me = self
        self.name = name
f = Fox("Sly")
assert f.me is f
assert f.__dict__['name'] == "Sly"
